extension_title: Intent.
text: I always scoff at the idea that internet addiction can even be a thing, much less something I myself have succumbed to, but the truth of the matter is, when I'm spending 7 hours a day on the computer with a decent chunk of it being mindless, I'm addicted. Intent has been the first step towards helping me become more aware of how I browse so I can choose to be more proactive my time spent online going forward. Thank you Kevin for the Elephant in the Brain, Melting Asphalt, and now, Intent.

extension_title: Intent.
text: Helpful in curbing many habits I have over using certain sites that, while useful at first, have since become a negative aspect of my life. I appreciate how this app presents itself as respectful of my time and helps guide me toward various features. I could see something like this just giving me all the tools upfront and throwing me into the deep end. But instead I actually feel like it's trying to be actively helpful in my goals. I'm very thankful.

text: This really fills the gap left when Clearly shut down, and it's far more flexible and effective. The developer is very active and responsive, especially on github (where the extension is developed). And you don't have to create an account and save pages to the cloud like some other extensions. It's easy enough to make quick edits to how you want the page to look with the editor in the top-right corner (look for the paintbrush, click on that). And there are all sorts of ways to adjust the stylesheet to render pages just as you want, if you don't mind digging into the stylesheet. Don't like your changes? You can always go back to the default stylesheet and start over. Or head over to the github page and look for others styelsheets that may fit your needs. If you read loads of articles on the web and want a dead simple way of making that easier and more tolerable, Just Read is an excellent option.

extension_title: Mercury Reader
text: I have been using Mercury Reader for over a year. If you want something to clean up the page you're on so you can read comfortably, now or later, then you will love this app too. By "later" I mean that I print to PDF to save an article or instructions for reference later, and I find it much easier to focus on the content later when I open it up by using Mercury. This can be important when my boss or other VIP want something done quickly that they know I "can do for them," maybe even on a 40-person conference call. Putting me on the spot? yeah. Putting their confidence in me? yeah. that too. Quick answers and action making them trust me more and more? yeah. 99% of the time, I just can't believe what a difference "white space" really makes when I'm reading... honestly, I used to pooh-pooh all that. But now I find myself staying on track more as well... without checking out the "Latest Star Wars Movie Preview" links in the sidebar. I suppose you're not reading this to be convinced of the value of a reader, but I'm leading up to the point that THIS reader has provided those "reader benefits" in a very solid manner for me for over the past year or so. And that 1% of the time when I get to answer my boss 5 seconds before anyone else does? Priceless. Does it sometimes think "the page" is only the first paragraph? Yes, rarely. But being involved in web-development, what we should be marveling at is HOW MANY different variations of webpage it DOES handle. When another FREE reader comes out that can read EVERY page ever coded perfectly... and which is used happily by so many others... well, then, sorry Mercury... I might move on, barring other considerations, and click that install button. Is the simple interface at times a tiny bit kludgy, with no instructions? yeah. Just keep clicking around. That's what I tell my sons. Don't give up just because you clicked once and what you wanted to happen didn't happen. Maybe the developer had a reason to tweak that expectation. For example, if you want to copy and paste just a sentence or word while in the reader, "selection" a.k.a. "highlighting" can be a bit frustrating at first. Just keep clicking. I realized each click did something different, and ALSO realized I liked the different things. First click selects text from bottom of page to top, or wherever you are at. This is useful, as one of the most common things users do, I'm sure, is copy and paste the entire article. With this, there's no more scrolling all the way down to the bottom of the page first. Just click, Ctrl/Cmd+'c', and go. Paste wherever you want. Second click I honestly forget, and I need to stop typing and get back to work, so... please add to comments below if you know, or I will try to remember to come back later, so check comments if interested. Third click "is the charm." This selects a single word, or inserts cursor, as one might expect from other programs, I believe. Whatever it does, it sets you up to select that single word or sentence that you wanted. Again... is there another FREE reader that can convert the readability of the page well, do everything else that Mercury can, and also allows you to customize how clicks work? I don't know of one yet. Until one comes out, or you learn of an existing one: just do it. Get Mercury Reader now.* *Yes, I am hoping that you'll download. So that they prosper and I can continue to reap the "reader benefits" I love. And, oh yeah, so you can benefit as well. That too. ;-P

extension_title: Block Site - Website Blocker for Chrome™
text: This is simple and easy to use but could use some modifications. One issue is that one main reason you use a blocker is to stop popups. When this blocks something it creates a popup you need to close. Also it doesn't tell you what it blocked where you could try to avoid a site. You only know it blocked something when you find the "blocking" popup underneath. One additional feature I would like to see is being able to use wildcards like *badsite* to take care of floating websites that subtly change their name. UPDATE: It appears that Chrome has completely redesigned the User Interface; UI, of Extensions. For Block Site it used to be obvious how to add a site to block. Since the UI is changed I can't detail it but when you first went in there was an obvious "Add Site to Block" option. Now when you go into More Tools -> Extensions, Scroll down to Extension Options and click on the icon on the right that looks like a square clock with a pointer (whatever that means) and you will now be in the screen that shows your previously selected blocked sites and have the option to add new ones. I kicked up the rating for Block Site because it appears that the problems relate to a Google Extension UI change. My job is 25 years in Software QA and this UI is really bad and I would not have released this product. I have been trying to get this to work for months after the change and just stumbled on how to get to actually looking at and adding sites. I guess this is a side effect of Open Source where there are volunteer developers but nobody with any QA or UI experience looking at these details. Another general Chrome issue is that it appears that each tab is a separate heavy-weight process as well as other utility processes. I currently have 6 tabs open and 26 Chrome processes in Task Manager. When adding these up I have often seen 5+ gigs used and even more since I have 16 gigs.. When added to the OS and other applications usage can get very high. If you have unlimited memory I guess this is OK but those with 4 gigs or less will probably get into real slowdowns if usage of disk swap space is necessary.

Now I cannot get it to appear blank, either. It now emphasizes that the page was blocked. While some may use this for kids, the previous version of this extension with the capability to block certain searches by keyword was perfect to allow some independence of a family member with mid-stage Alzheimer's disease. It was great for keeping them away from the sites where they would forget they already paid for something, and would purchase it again. And again. And again. On different websites, too. Yes, the website blocker does work. But it is NOWHERE near as helpful as the keyword blocker was. I don't know how to block every website on that topic, nor do I have the time. In regards to the rating, the extension is well organized. It is simple to use, and easy to navigate. As well, it is not cluttered and each section is quickly explained. I like that it has the different sections for sites, work, and adults. A majority of the rating was taken away BECAUSE of the keyword feature no longer being accessible. I'm sure there are legal reasons for the removal of this feature, as well. I also rated this application lower because of the inability to block a website without it showing that the website is blocked. That is something I did not see on the earlier version. As bummed as I am about the changes, thank you for taking the time to create this application. While it no longer serves the purpose that I needed it to, I really did like it.

extension_title: Block Site - Website Blocker for Chrome™
text: When I first installed this extension, it was perfect. They've made some changes recently that negatively affect what made this extension so much more useful than other similar ones. You used to be able to set specific block time intervals for individual websites. Now, you can only set one interval per individual website. This was probably the best feature of Block Site and it's frustrating they've removed it. I like to allow access to some blocked sites during my lunch break, but my schedule varies every day - now I can no longer vary the un-blocked time to correspond to my schedule. In the general setting for active days and times, you can pick multiple time intervals for different days, but the list of intervals you selected only displays the time, not the day. So it's impossible to tell which days you've set your blocks for already. In order to make this work, I'll have to make a note somewhere else about the order I added the intervals so I know which days they correspond to. That's REALLY annoying! The time interval settings are what really set Block Site apart from other similar apps. I would give it a resounding 5 stars if they restored the time interval functionality to what it was a couple months ago.

text: This is a great extension, but it would be better if there are individual groups of webpages where you can customize them. For example, it would be better if we can block a set of webpages {A} during this time period, allow a different set of webpages {B} during another time period, and blocking a third set of webpages {C} during another time period, and so on. It would also be great if we could customize the blocked words in a similar fashion. That way, we can specifically allow some sites during certain times while others during other times. The existing "Domains" option does not offer the option to both block and allow the webpage and is also inconvenient - it would be much easier to quickly copy-paste a set of webpages onto a plain textbox and apply settings to them as a whole. Another issue is that some sites, like chrome://extension, cannot be blocked (that particular site requires the full version). Generally, though, the extension works very well. extension_title: Block Site - Website Blocker for Chrome™
text: I've had it 5 minutes and I already have some key concerns. First, it does not handle new gTLDs, like .click, .club, or .wtf. There are hundreds of gTLDs now and, apparently, Block Site is unaware of them and won't let you enter a URL using one of them, so installmalware.click, for instance, cannot be blocked with this extension. The other issue is I tried to report this in feedback, typed in the issue and my email address and clicked "Submit" and got a 404 error! (Perhaps because my email uses one of these gTLDs?) Also, it does not block blacklisted URLs in pop-ups. I also found if a site pops up a dialog box when onClose is called, this extension sets up a vicious cycle: The site opens in a tab, Block Site closes it, thus triggering onClose, and if the site tries to re-open in another window, it repeats. This could go on forever if one does not use Chrome's Task Manager to kill tabs. (In other words, Block Site blocks a site *after* it is loaded, not before it is loaded, which allows the site to do things we might not want it to do before Block Site takes over.) These first two mistakes are ones any programmer who has been working for over a year or so should have avoided.

text: I like it. It keeps tab clutter down without requiring my attention, and makes it easy to dig out from under the pile of tabs I had open without forgetting any. Many similar extensions require your time and attention to manage and organize tabs, while claiming to save your time by organizing them. This runs in the background, never needing your input until you're ready to start digging out the backlogs of sites you didn't have time for before. There are features I feel would be helpful here, though. Little things that would be helpful. An option to lock ALL tabs except those configured, instead of only those configured. Mark the tabs that are locked, with an additional indicator when a tab is auto-locked, as opposed to manual. Shortcuts to lock tabs. Sorting in the tab list, like alphabetically(by site). extension_title: Tab Wrangler
text: I am a big fan of Tab Suspender, but I decided to give this extension a try. Surely this must save more memory compared to the Suspender extension. This one actually closes and saves the tabs, whereas Suspender simply "freezes" each tab without actually closing it. Imagine my surprise when Wrangler had 15 open tabs, and 8 of them closed+saved, my memory usage was 2.9GB My memory usage with 15 tabs open with Suspender? 2.4GB To top it off, I HATE how this extension closes my tabs and causes confusion. Sure, they're saved onto a list, but it's incredibly difficult to look at that list to determine where all the tabs were previously, and trying to reorder them is a chore. With other extensions that simply freeze each tab without closing them, I don't have to worry about saving them, closing them, or reopening them. Lastly, unlike OneTab or Session Buddy, this extension doesn't make it obvious how to have the saved tabs page open. Clicking the favicon opens a popup menu instead of the page in a new tab. extension_title: Dayboard: New Tab & Site Blocker
text: I quite like it, in general it's pretty useful. However, I have been running into a couple annoyances which have made me look for alternatives to compliment using Dayboard. I understand that one should not do too many tasks on one day. Having 5 core tasks per day is great. However, I also have some (important) chores I am listing. I therefore find that 5 tasks is too few for my use. I was looking for an option to change this number, but it does not seem to exist. If it does, please let me know and I will change my review accordingly. Another thing I miss is the ability to kind of schedule tasks. I like it that I can create tasks for tomorrow, but what about "this week". For starters it would be awesome if we can have a list of todo's that are neither today/tomorrow. It's just an unscheduled list. From that list, we can then drag them to today/tomorrow. That way, it also solves the 5-a-day problem. As I can drag new todo's into my day when I have finished my 5. Right now, I find myself having to have a secondary todo list in another app to ensure I don't forget stuff I didn't manage to fit in my today/tomorrow list. I really love the forbidden-sites feature. However, I usually take a 1.5-2 hour lunch/distraction break. I have had many times where I got the popup that blocks the website while I was allowing myself to at the moment. The only option I had was to "continue working" or "done for the day". I would love to see a "Taking a xxx minute break" option (possibly also a configurable setting to only allow 1-3 breaks a day, with a total of 30-90 minutes or so). You could even let this popup show whenever you visit a forbidden website. A countdown to allowable minutes would be handy too, so you know you "relax allowance" instead of being surprised with a popup. I have had to select "done for the day" a couple of times already in the middle of the day, defeating the point of it as it would not help me focus the rest of the day. Finally, the todo popup on each page load is quite useful as well. It would be great though if it does not open up again when browsing the same website (domain) and it should be limited (across multiple tabs) to only pop-up every minute or so. The snooze is fine, but I find myself snoozing it too often just because the popup bothers me when I have opened up many tabs from say a google search. Overall I really think Dayboard has a lot of potential. So far the only tool I found that helps you fight distractions. It just needs a bit of ironing out, and hopefully some additional task features. If the above points get improved I think I would also be happy to pay for it, and of-course to give it a higher rating :-)

extension_title: Dayboard: New Tab & Site Blocker
text: This is a great tool. Taking 5 minutes in the morning to curate my most important tasks helps give me perspective and takes the thinking out of trying to decide what I should work on next. Seeing it every time I open a new tab helps me keep that perspective and not get too carried away working on a low priority task. This team has the best support I've ever seen. No matter when I e-mail them, I have received thoughtful, helpful, human replies within 20 minutes at the absolute most. Such a joy to interact with. Features I would still like: 1) A way to retroactively mark completion of a task. If I finish a task at 12:01am on Wednesday, I want to be able to mark it as a task that I completed Tuesday so it will show up as crossed off in Tuesday's list and will not take up space on Wednesday's list. Currently it shows as completed on Wednesday, and I could delete it to free up a slot but that's a shame since it undermines my ability to see my history by flipping through past days. A completed task will still show in history even if it's deleted, but I like flipping through the days because I can see my completed tasks in context with the incomplete ones. Retroactive completion would also help me fill in gaps in the history when I work offline for a couple days and come back to find that my list is full of tasks that I finished while offline. 2) An option to display the team rather than my personal list when I open a new tab. 3) A Firefox version of the extension. I'm using Chrome only because it has a better Dayboard experience, and I would love to be able to switch back to my preferred browser.

And also, I found this while I was reading, that the timer ends early. It is supposed to end at the end of Homestuck, supposedly the credits, right? Well really, once the timer was at 0 hours and then disappeared, I still had hours left to read. The timer gives you an idea and a goal to work towards but it is certainly not an accurate measurement. I assumed this happened because the plugin was developed before Homestuck was finished? All in all, it's no problem. This is the best Homestuck plugin.

text: The idea of this extension is very good, I like it! But there is an important missing feature: Most users have procrastination issues which make them postpone the moment in which they will click on the "Start focusing" button. Therefore those users (including me) will get distracted and they will click on that button after several hours, or even never, sometimes wasting a whole working day. I would suggest, for these people, to add an optional setting where they can set a timer after which they will be forced to start focusing. They will be happy, before starting, to set this timer and just look to a couple of youtube videos or news, until suddenly they are automatically stopped and they realize it's time to focus!
